title: Helm: Install, Configure and Operate
subtitle: Charts, releases, values, upgrades and production practice
description: Learn Helm 3 from zero: what charts and releases are, how to find and read charts, install them with values files, inspect and operate releases, upgrade and roll back safely, clean up, and run Helm with production discipline.
outcomes: Explain charts, releases, repositories, values and revisions
Find, read and install charts with --set and values files
Upgrade, roll back and uninstall releases safely with --atomic and --wait
Apply production practices: version pinning, per-environment values, diff and OCI
Troubleshoot failed, pending and conflicting releases

modules.title: Helm foundations
modules.summary: The vocabulary, the client and finding charts.

lessons.title: Why Helm: charts, releases and values
lessons.summary: What problem Helm solves, the five core words (chart, release, repository, values, revision) and how to install the Helm CLI.
objectives: Explain the problem Helm solves compared with plain kubectl apply
Define chart, release, repository, values and revision with an example of each
Install the Helm 3 client and verify it can reach your cluster
Describe what a chart directory contains

sections.title: What you will build and the path through this course
sections.body:
In this course you start with an empty cluster and a laptop and end by operating a real application, an **nginx web server from the bitnami/nginx chart**, the way a production team does: installed with a values file, inspected, upgraded safely, rolled back, cleaned up and troubleshot when it fails.

The path has three modules. **Foundations** (this lesson and the next) defines the vocabulary and shows how to find charts. **Releases** covers installing, inspecting, upgrading, rolling back and uninstalling. **Production** covers version pinning, per-environment values, secrets, the diff plugin, OCI registries and a troubleshooting playbook. Every lesson builds on the previous one, so follow them in order. You should already know Deployments, Services and ConfigMaps from the Workloads course.

**The problem Helm solves:** a real application needs a Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap and more, copied per environment with image tags and replica counts edited by hand, with no record of what is installed. **Helm** is the package manager for Kubernetes: it bundles manifests as templates, fills them from a few settings, installs them as one named unit and remembers every change so you can upgrade or roll back with one command. Helm 3 is client-only (no server in the cluster) and uses the same kubeconfig as kubectl.

sections.title: The five words you must know
head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: A package: a directory (or .tgz) of templates plus default settings and metadata
One installed instance of a chart in a cluster and namespace, with a name you choose
web (nginx chart installed in namespace demo)
An HTTP (or OCI) location that serves an index of charts
The settings that fill the templates; chart defaults overridden by your --set or -f
A numbered snapshot of a release; every install, upgrade or rollback adds one

sections.title: About this example: a minimal chart layout
sections.body: This is what `helm create web` generates, shown as a tree. A chart is only a folder with a fixed shape. Look at **Chart.yaml** (name and version), **values.yaml** (the defaults) and the **templates/** directory (the Kubernetes manifests with Go template placeholders). You will not write charts in this course, but knowing the layout lets you read any chart you install.

sections.title: chart layout
sections.code:
web/
├── Chart.yaml          # name, chart version, app version, description
├── values.yaml         # default values (the knobs users can turn)
├── charts/             # dependency charts (subcharts)
├── templates/
│   ├── deployment.yaml # template: image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}
│   ├── service.yaml
│   ├── ingress.yaml
│   ├── _helpers.tpl    # reusable template snippets
│   └── NOTES.txt       # message printed after install
└── .helmignore
sections.output:
$ helm create web
Creating web
sections.note: Templates use Go template syntax: {{ .Values.x }} reads a value, {{ .Release.Name }} reads the release name.

sections.title: About this example: Chart.yaml
sections.body: Chart.yaml is the identity card of a chart and is read by `helm show chart`. Note that there are **two** versions: `version` is the version of the chart packaging itself (it changes when templates change) and `appVersion` is the version of the software inside (here nginx). They move independently, which confuses many beginners.

sections.title: Chart.yaml
sections.code:
apiVersion: v2
name: nginx
description: NGINX Open Source is a web server
type: application
version: 18.2.4        # chart version: use this when pinning
appVersion: 1.27.1     # nginx version shipped by default
keywords:
  - nginx
  - http
  - web
maintainers:
  - name: Broadcom, Inc. All Rights Reserved.
kubeVersion: '>=1.23.0-0'
sections.note: apiVersion: v2 means a Helm 3 chart.

sections.title: About this example: installing the Helm client
sections.body: Helm is a single binary. The official install script detects your OS and puts `helm` in /usr/local/bin; package managers such as Homebrew, apt (Helm's official repo), Chocolatey and snap also work. After installing, `helm version` confirms the client, and `helm env` shows where Helm keeps its cache and config. Run these on the machine where kubectl already works.

sections.title: install and verify Helm
sections.code:
curl -fsSL -o get_helm.sh https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3
chmod 700 get_helm.sh
./get_helm.sh
helm version --short
kubectl config current-context
helm env | grep -E 'HELM_(NAMESPACE|KUBECONTEXT|CACHE_HOME|CONFIG_HOME)'
sections.output:
Downloading https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.16.2-linux-amd64.tar.gz
Verifying checksum... Done.
Preparing to install helm into /usr/local/bin
helm installed into /usr/local/bin/helm
v3.16.2+g13654a5
kind-opsdeck
HELM_CACHE_HOME="/home/ali/.cache/helm"
HELM_CONFIG_HOME="/home/ali/.config/helm"
HELM_KUBECONTEXT=""
HELM_NAMESPACE=""
sections.note: Helm uses the current kubectl context. Override with --kube-context and -n/--namespace per command.

sections.title: Common mistake: installing into the wrong cluster
sections.body: Helm acts on whatever `kubectl config current-context` points to, with no confirmation. Before any `helm install` or `helm upgrade` on a shared machine, run `kubectl config current-context` or pass `--kube-context` explicitly. Helm 2 needed a server component called Tiller; Helm 3 removed it, so ignore old tutorials that mention `helm init` or Tiller.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Helm packages manifests as a **chart**, fills them with **values**, installs them as a named **release** in a namespace, and records each change as a **revision**. A **repository** is where charts are published. The Helm 3 client needs only a kubeconfig and is now installed. Next lesson: adding repositories, searching for charts and reading a chart's documentation and default values before installing it.

exercises.expected: A Helm 3 version string such as v3.16.2+g13654a5, then your context name.
exercises.hint: helm version without --short prints a Go struct.

exercises.title: Scaffold a chart

exercises.command: cd /tmp && helm create demo && ls demo demo/templates
exercises.expected: Chart.yaml, values.yaml, charts and templates, with deployment.yaml inside templates.
exercises.hint: helm create writes into the current directory.

questions.question: What is a Helm release?
options: A chart packaged as a .tgz file
A named installed instance of a chart in a namespace
questions.explain: A release is created by helm install and is identified by name and namespace; the same chart can be installed many times as different releases.

questions.question: Which component does Helm 3 require inside the cluster?
questions.explain: Tiller was removed in Helm 3. The client uses your kubeconfig and stores release state as Secrets.

questions.question: What is the difference between chart version and appVersion?
options: version is the packaging version, appVersion the software version inside
questions.explain: Chart `version` changes when the chart changes; `appVersion` describes the packaged application and is informational.

questions.question: Which file holds the default settings of a chart?
questions.explain: values.yaml provides defaults that --set and -f override.

lessons.title: Repositories, searching and reading a chart
lessons.summary: Add repositories, search them and Artifact Hub, and use helm show to read a chart's metadata, README and default values before installing.
objectives: Add, update, list and remove chart repositories
Search added repositories with helm search repo and the public catalog with helm search hub
List available versions of a chart
Read chart info with helm show chart, readme, values and all

sections.title: Repositories are just an index plus archives
sections.body:
A chart repository is a web server that exposes an `index.yaml` file listing every chart and version, and the packaged `.tgz` archives it points to. `helm repo add` stores the name and URL locally in your Helm config; `helm repo update` downloads each index into the local cache. Searching and installing then work from that cached index, which is why you must update before looking for new versions.

A repository **name** is a local alias you choose (`bitnami`). Charts are then referred to as `REPO/CHART`, for example `bitnami/nginx`.

sections.title: About this example: adding a repository
sections.body: These commands register the Bitnami repository, refresh the local index and list what is configured. The `helm repo list` output shows the alias and URL; the alias is the first half of every `bitnami/...` reference you use later. Run them once per machine.

sections.title: helm repo add, update, list
sections.code:
helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update
helm repo list
sections.output:
"bitnami" has been added to your repositories
"ingress-nginx" has been added to your repositories
Hang tight while we grab the latest from your chart repositories...
...Successfully got an update from the "ingress-nginx" chart repository
...Successfully got an update from the "bitnami" chart repository
Update Complete. ⎈Happy Helming!⎈
NAME            URL
bitnami         https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
ingress-nginx   https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx

sections.title: About this example: searching your repositories
sections.body: `helm search repo` searches only the repositories you added and reads the local cache. Without flags it shows the latest version of each match. The columns are the full chart name, the chart version, the app version and the description. Add `--versions` to see every published version, which you need when pinning.

sections.title: helm search repo
sections.code:
helm search repo nginx
helm search repo bitnami/nginx --versions | head -5
sections.output:

bitnami/nginx-ingress-controller 11.4.3         1.11.2          NGINX Ingress Controller is an Ingress control...
ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx     4.11.3          1.11.3          Ingress controller for Kubernetes using NGINX a...

sections.note: Development and pre-release versions are hidden unless you add --devel.

sections.title: About this example: reading a chart before installing it
sections.body: `helm show` prints information about a chart without installing anything: `chart` is Chart.yaml, `readme` the documentation, `values` the full default values and `all` everything. The values file is the most important: it is the complete list of settings you can override. Save it to a file; it becomes the starting point of your own values file in the next lesson.

sections.title: helm show
sections.code:
helm show chart bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4 | head -8
helm show values bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4 > nginx-defaults.yaml
grep -nE '^(replicaCount|service:|  type:|  port|image:|  tag)' nginx-defaults.yaml | head
helm show readme bitnami/nginx | head -3
sections.output:
annotations:
  category: Infrastructure
apiVersion: v2
appVersion: 1.27.1
description: NGINX Open Source is a web server that can be also used as a reverse proxy
53:image:
55:  tag: 1.27.1-debian-12-r2
188:replicaCount: 1
380:service:
382:  type: LoadBalancer
# NGINX Open Source packaged by Bitnami
sections.note: Always pass --version; otherwise Helm shows the newest chart, which may differ from the one you run.

sections.title: Common mistake: forgetting helm repo update
sections.body: If a chart version you were told exists does not appear in `helm search repo`, your cached index is stale. Run `helm repo update` first. Also remember that publishers can change policies: the Bitnami public catalog changed in 2025, so verify in the chart README which image registry and tags a chart uses before relying on it in production.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You can now add and refresh repositories, search them with `helm search repo` (and the public catalog with `helm search hub`), list versions with `--versions`, and read a chart's defaults with `helm show values`. Next lesson turns this reading into action: installing the nginx chart as a release, overriding values with `--set` and `-f`, choosing a namespace and previewing with `--dry-run` and `helm template`.

questions.question: Which command searches only repositories you have added?
questions.explain: helm search repo reads the local cache of added repos; search hub queries Artifact Hub.

questions.question: Why run helm repo update?
options: To refresh the cached index of chart versions
questions.explain: It downloads each repo's index.yaml so searches and installs see new versions.

questions.question: Which command prints the default settings of a chart?
questions.explain: helm get values reads an installed release; helm show values reads the chart.

questions.question: How do you list all versions of a chart?
questions.explain: --versions disables the default 'latest only' behaviour.

modules.title: Working with releases
modules.summary: Install, inspect, upgrade, roll back and remove.

lessons.title: Installing a release step by step
lessons.summary: Install bitnami/nginx, override values with --set and -f, target a namespace, and preview with --dry-run, --debug and helm template.
objectives: Run helm install with a release name, chart and version
Override values with --set and a values file and know their precedence
Create the namespace with --create-namespace
Preview output safely with --dry-run=server, --debug and helm template

sections.title: Anatomy of helm install
sections.body:
`helm install RELEASE_NAME CHART` renders the chart's templates with the effective values, sends the resulting manifests to the API server and records the release as revision 1. The release name must be unique inside its namespace. Namespaces are **not** created by the chart: you pass `-n NAMESPACE` and, if it does not exist, `--create-namespace`.

Before installing for real, write down four decisions: the release name (`web`), the chart and version (`bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4`), the namespace (`demo`) and your value overrides. The following examples go from the simplest form to the production form.

sections.title: About this example: a values file
sections.body: A values file is plain YAML that mirrors the structure of the chart's values.yaml; you only include keys you change, and Helm merges them over the defaults. Keep it in Git next to your deployment code. Because it is a fragment of a chart configuration and not a Kubernetes object, it is shown as text.

sections.title: values-demo.yaml
sections.code:
replicaCount: 2

service:
  type: ClusterIP

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 50m
    memory: 64Mi
  limits:
    memory: 128Mi

podLabels:
  team: platform

serverBlock: |-
  server {
    listen 8080;
    location / { return 200 'hello from helm\n'; add_header Content-Type text/plain; }
    location /healthz { return 200 'ok'; }
  }
sections.note: Maps are merged key by key; lists are replaced entirely, not merged.

sections.title: About this example: installing with a values file
sections.body: Here `-f` points to the file above. When you pass several `-f` files, later files win, and `--set` wins over every file. This is the precedence chain: chart defaults, then each -f in order, then --set. `--wait` makes Helm wait until Pods are ready, and `--timeout` caps the wait.

sections.title: helm install -f
sections.code:
helm install web bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4 -n demo --create-namespace \
  -f values-demo.yaml --wait --timeout 3m
kubectl get deploy web-nginx -n demo
sections.output:
NAME: web
LAST DEPLOYED: Thu Nov 13 10:30:19 2026
NAMESPACE: demo
STATUS: deployed
REVISION: 1
TEST SUITE: None
NAME        READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
web-nginx   2/2     2            2           15m

sections.title: Install flags you will use daily
head: Flag
What it does
Example
rows: Wait for readiness, bound the wait
Render without installing; server also validates against the API
Roll back automatically on failure (see upgrades lesson)

sections.title: About this example: previewing with helm template
sections.body: `helm template` renders the chart locally and prints the manifests without contacting the cluster, so it works in CI and lets you review exactly what would be created. This is the rendered Service for our values: `type: ClusterIP` came from values-demo.yaml and the labels from the chart's helpers. Pipe it to `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -` for API validation.

sections.title: helm template and --dry-run
sections.code:
helm template web bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4 -n demo -f values-demo.yaml \
  --show-only templates/svc.yaml
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-demo.yaml --dry-run=server --debug | head -12
sections.output:
---
# Source: nginx/templates/svc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-nginx
  namespace: "demo"
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/instance: web
    app.kubernetes.io/name: nginx
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
install.go:225: [debug] Original chart version: ""
install.go:242: [debug] CHART PATH: /home/ali/.cache/helm/repository/nginx-18.2.4.tgz

NAME: web
STATUS: pending-install
REVISION: 1
sections.note: helm template does not know cluster capabilities; add --validate or --api-versions if a chart branches on them.

sections.title: Common mistake: dry-run that hides problems
sections.body: `--dry-run=client` (the old default) never asks the API server, so errors such as an unknown API version or an existing object with a conflicting owner appear only on the real install. Use `--dry-run=server` for the closest rehearsal, and add `--debug` to print the computed values and rendered manifests.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: `helm install RELEASE CHART -n NS --create-namespace --version X -f values.yaml` is the production shape; `helm upgrade --install` makes it idempotent. Values precedence is chart defaults, then `-f` files in order, then `--set`. Preview with `helm template` or `--dry-run=server --debug`. Next lesson: inspect the release you created with `helm list`, `status`, `get` and `history`.

questions.question: Which has the highest precedence?
questions.explain: Order is defaults, -f files left to right, then --set.

questions.question: What does helm upgrade --install do?
questions.explain: It is the idempotent deployment command.

questions.question: Which flag creates the target namespace?
questions.explain: -n only selects the namespace; --create-namespace creates it.

questions.question: Which command renders manifests without a cluster connection?
questions.explain: helm template is purely local.

lessons.title: Inspecting and operating releases
lessons.summary: Use helm list, status, get values, manifest, notes and hooks, and history to know exactly what is deployed and how it got there.
objectives: List releases across namespaces and read each column
Read release status and the deployed notes
Retrieve user-supplied versus computed values and the exact manifest
Read the revision history of a release

sections.title: Where Helm stores release state
sections.body: Helm keeps each revision of a release as a Kubernetes **Secret** of type `helm.sh/release.v1` in the release's namespace, named `sh.helm.release.v1.RELEASE.vREVISION`. It contains the chart, the values and the rendered manifest, compressed. This is why Helm needs no server and why `helm list` only needs access to Secrets in the namespace. You can see them with kubectl, but you should read them through Helm commands instead.

sections.title: About this example: helm list
sections.body: `helm list` shows releases in the current namespace; `-A` shows all namespaces; `-a` includes failed and uninstalled ones and `--failed` or `--pending` filters by state. Check **STATUS** first: anything other than deployed needs attention. **CHART** is name-version and **APP VERSION** the software version.

sections.title: helm list
sections.code:
helm list -A
helm list -n demo --output yaml | head -9
helm status web -n demo | head -6
sections.output:

web       demo       3         2026-11-13 10:30:19.4 +0000 UTC          deployed  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1
ingress   ingress    1         2026-11-12 16:02:55.1 +0000 UTC          deployed  ingress-nginx-4.11.3  1.11.3
- app_version: 1.27.1
  chart: nginx-18.2.4
  name: web
  namespace: demo
  revision: "3"
  status: deployed

LAST DEPLOYED: Thu Nov 13 10:30:19 2026
NAMESPACE: demo

sections.title: About this example: helm get values and manifest
sections.body: `helm get values` prints only what **you** supplied (the overrides); adding `--all` also prints the merged chart defaults. `helm get manifest` prints the exact YAML that Helm applied for the current revision, and `--revision N` reads an older one. Use these to answer 'what is really deployed?' without trusting your memory or the repository.

sections.title: helm get
sections.code:
helm get values web -n demo
helm get values web -n demo --all | head -5
helm get manifest web -n demo | grep -E '^(kind|  name):' | head -6
helm get all web -n demo --revision 1 | head -3
sections.output:
USER-SUPPLIED VALUES:
podLabels:
  team: platform
replicaCount: 2
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 128Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 50m
    memory: 64Mi
service:
  type: ClusterIP
COMPUTED VALUES:
affinity: {}
architecture: standalone
kind: Deployment
  name: web-nginx
kind: Service
  name: web-nginx
NAME: web
LAST DEPLOYED: Thu Nov 13 10:15:42 2026
NAMESPACE: demo

sections.title: About this example: helm history
sections.body: `helm history` lists every revision with its status and a description. Statuses: `deployed` (live), `superseded` (replaced by a newer one), `failed`, `uninstalled`, `pending-*` (an operation is in flight or crashed). The history is your audit trail and the menu for rollbacks in the next lesson. Helm keeps 10 revisions by default; change that with `--history-max`.

sections.title: helm history
sections.code: helm history web -n demo
sections.output:
REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART         APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
1         Thu Nov 13 10:15:42 2026  superseded  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Install complete
2         Thu Nov 13 10:22:07 2026  superseded  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Upgrade complete
3         Thu Nov 13 10:30:19 2026  deployed    nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Upgrade complete

sections.title: Release states
head: Status
Meaning
What to do
rows: Install or upgrade did not complete
Read the error, fix, upgrade or rollback
An operation is running or was interrupted
Wait; if stuck see troubleshooting lesson
Removal in progress or kept by --keep-history

sections.title: Compare live objects with the release
sections.body: `helm get manifest web -n demo | kubectl diff -f -` shows differences between what Helm believes it deployed and the cluster. Differences mean someone ran `kubectl edit` by hand; the next `helm upgrade` will overwrite them in most cases.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: `helm list` finds releases, `helm status` shows health and notes, `helm get values/manifest/notes/all` show what was configured and applied, and `helm history` is the audit trail. All state lives in Secrets in the release namespace. Next lesson: changing a live release safely with `helm upgrade`, the `--reuse-values` trap, `--atomic`, `--wait`, `--timeout` and `helm rollback`.

lessons.title: Upgrading, rolling back and uninstalling
lessons.summary: Change a live release safely: --reuse-values versus --reset-values, --atomic, --wait, rollback, and a clean uninstall including PVCs and CRDs.
objectives: Upgrade a release and understand how values are merged
Choose between --reuse-values, --reset-values and --reset-then-reuse-values
Use --wait, --timeout and --atomic to make upgrades safe
Roll back to a previous revision
Uninstall, use --keep-history and clean up PVCs and CRDs

sections.title: How upgrade computes values
sections.body:
`helm upgrade RELEASE CHART` renders a new revision and applies it as a three-way merge between the old manifest, the live state and the new manifest. The value handling is the part that surprises people. **By default, upgrade resets to the new chart's defaults and applies only the values you pass this time**; settings from the previous install are forgotten unless you pass them again. Two flags change that:

- `--reuse-values` reuses the previous revision's computed values and merges your new ones on top. New defaults added by a newer chart version are **ignored**, which can break upgrades.
- `--reset-values` explicitly resets to the new chart defaults, then applies what you pass.
- `--reset-then-reuse-values` (Helm 3.14+) resets to new chart defaults, then re-applies your previously supplied values, then your new ones. This is usually what people mean by reuse.

sections.title: Value handling during upgrade
head: Flag
Starting point
Risk
rows: New chart defaults + values you pass now
Previous overrides silently lost if not re-passed
Last revision's computed values + new ones
New chart defaults missing, rendering errors after chart bumps
New defaults + last user values + new ones
Best of both; needs Helm 3.14 or newer

sections.title: About this example: a failing upgrade with --atomic
sections.body: Here an invalid image tag makes the new Pods hang in ImagePullBackOff. Helm waits until the timeout, then automatically restores the previous revision and records both events. The error line tells you why it failed and the history shows the failed revision followed by the rollback. Without --atomic, the release would stay `failed` with broken Pods running.

sections.title: atomic failure and auto rollback
sections.code:
helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-demo.yaml \
  --set image.tag=does-not-exist --atomic --timeout 90s
helm history web -n demo | tail -3
sections.output:
Error: UPGRADE FAILED: release web failed, and has been rolled back due to atomic being set: context deadline exceeded
REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART         APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
4         Thu Nov 13 11:02:14 2026  superseded  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Upgrade complete
5         Thu Nov 13 11:09:40 2026  failed      nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Upgrade "web" failed: context deadline exceeded
6         Thu Nov 13 11:11:12 2026  deployed    nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Rollback to 4

sections.title: About this example: manual rollback
sections.body: `helm rollback RELEASE REVISION` creates a **new** revision whose content is a copy of the chosen old one; history only grows. Omit the revision number to go back one step. Add `--wait` so the command returns when Pods are ready, and `--cleanup-on-fail` to delete resources created during a failed rollback. Rollback restores Kubernetes objects, not data inside PVCs or databases.

sections.title: helm rollback
sections.code:
helm rollback web 3 -n demo --wait --timeout 3m
helm history web -n demo | tail -2
sections.output:
Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS      CHART         APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
6         Thu Nov 13 11:11:12 2026  superseded  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Rollback to 4
7         Thu Nov 13 11:15:03 2026  deployed    nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Rollback to 3

sections.title: About this example: what uninstall leaves behind
sections.body: This example first uninstalls a release named db (a database chart) with --keep-history, then looks for what Helm left behind. Helm deletes objects it created from templates, but **not** PersistentVolumeClaims created by StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates, not CRDs installed from a chart's `crds/` directory, and not the namespace. Look for leftovers by the release label and clean them deliberately: deleting a PVC deletes data, so confirm first.

sections.title: post-uninstall cleanup
sections.code:
helm uninstall db -n demo --keep-history
kubectl get pvc,secret -n demo -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=db
kubectl delete pvc -n demo -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=db
kubectl get crd | grep -i monitoring.coreos.com
kubectl delete namespace demo
sections.output:
release "db" uninstalled
NAME                                STATUS   VOLUME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   AGE
persistentvolumeclaim/data-db-0     Bound    pvc-9a1c…   8Gi        RWO            2d
persistentvolumeclaim "data-db-0" deleted
alertmanagerconfigs.monitoring.coreos.com   2026-11-01T08:00:00Z
namespace "demo" deleted
sections.note: CRDs are shared cluster-wide; deleting one deletes every custom resource of that kind in all namespaces.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: 1) Upgrading without re-passing earlier --set values, which silently reverts them. 2) Using --reuse-values across chart version bumps. 3) Upgrading without --wait or --atomic and believing 'deployed' means healthy. 4) Deleting CRDs or PVCs to 'clean up' without checking what else uses them. 5) Expecting rollback to undo database migrations or data changes.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Keep all values in files and pass them on every `helm upgrade`; prefer `--reset-then-reuse-values` to `--reuse-values` if you must reuse. Use `--atomic --timeout` for safe upgrades, `helm rollback` to go to an earlier revision (a new revision is created), and `helm uninstall [--keep-history]` followed by deliberate PVC and CRD cleanup. Next: production practices that make all of this repeatable across environments.

exercises.title: Break and recover
exercises.prompt: Upgrade web with a nonexistent image tag using --atomic and a 60s timeout, then check history.
exercises.command: helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-demo.yaml --set image.tag=nope --atomic --timeout 60s; helm history web -n demo
exercises.expected: Error ... rolled back; history shows a failed revision then a rollback revision.
exercises.hint: Pods will sit in ImagePullBackOff until the timeout.
exercises.solution: helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-demo.yaml --set image.tag=nope --atomic --timeout 60s

exercises.title: Uninstall with history
exercises.prompt: Uninstall web keeping history, list uninstalled releases, then roll it back to life.
exercises.command: helm uninstall web -n demo --keep-history && helm list -n demo --uninstalled && helm rollback web -n demo
exercises.expected: The release returns to deployed with a new revision.
exercises.hint: Only works if history was kept.
exercises.solution: helm uninstall web -n demo --keep-history; helm rollback web -n demo

questions.question: What does a plain helm upgrade do with values from the previous install?
questions.explain: Without --reuse-values, previous overrides are not retained.

questions.question: What does --atomic do?
options: Rolls back automatically on failure and implies --wait
questions.explain: It restores the previous revision if the upgrade fails or times out.

questions.question: After helm rollback web 3, what happens to history?
options: A new revision is added copying revision 3
questions.explain: Rollback creates a new revision.

questions.question: Which is usually left after helm uninstall of a StatefulSet chart?
questions.explain: PVCs from volumeClaimTemplates are kept to protect data.

lessons.title: Production practices: versions, environments, secrets, diff and OCI
lessons.summary: Make Helm deployments repeatable: pin versions, layer values per environment, handle secrets, preview changes with helm diff and use OCI registries.
objectives: Pin chart versions and image tags
Structure values files per environment and layer them
Keep secrets out of Git and out of values
Preview upgrades with the helm diff plugin
Pull and install charts from an OCI registry

sections.title: About this example: values layered per environment
sections.body: Pin the image tag in the base file and pass `--version` for the chart on every deploy. Keep one shared base file and one small file per environment containing only differences. Because later `-f` files win and maps merge key by key, `values-prod.yaml` stays short. Remember lists are replaced wholesale, so avoid putting lists in the base if environments need to extend them.

sections.title: values per environment
sections.code:
# values-base.yaml (shared)
image:
  tag: 1.27.1-debian-12-r2   # pinned, never latest
replicaCount: 2
service:
  type: ClusterIP
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi }

# values-staging.yaml
replicaCount: 2

# values-prod.yaml
replicaCount: 6
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
  limits: { memory: 512Mi }
podDisruptionBudget:
  create: true
  minAvailable: 4

sections.title: About this example: the helm diff plugin
sections.body: `helm diff` is a community plugin (databus23/helm-diff) that compares a proposed upgrade with the live release and prints a colored diff of rendered manifests, like `terraform plan`. Install it once, then run it in CI on every pull request. Lines starting with `-` are removed, `+` are added; here only replicas and a PDB change, so the change is safe to approve.

sections.title: helm diff upgrade
sections.code:
helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff
helm diff upgrade web bitnami/nginx --version 18.2.4 -n prod \
  -f values-base.yaml -f values-prod.yaml --context 2
sections.output:
Successfully installed plugin: diff
prod, web-nginx, Deployment (apps) has changed:
  spec:
-   replicas: 2
+   replicas: 6
prod, web-nginx, PodDisruptionBudget (policy) has been added:
+ spec:
+   minAvailable: 4
sections.note: Add --detailed-exitcode in CI: exit 2 means changes exist.

sections.title: About this example: referencing an existing Secret
sections.body: Values are stored in plain text inside the release Secret and are visible to `helm get values`, so never commit passwords in values files; reference a Secret that lives outside Helm (or use External Secrets, the Secrets Store CSI driver, or SOPS with helm-secrets). This manifest is the Secret you create outside Helm (with SealedSecrets, External Secrets or kubectl). The chart's values then only contain its name. Check the chart README for the exact key (`auth.existingSecret`, `existingSecret` and so on) since it differs per chart.

sections.title: web-credentials Secret
sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: web-credentials
  namespace: demo
type: Opaque
stringData:
  password: change-me-in-real-life
  token: example-token
sections.output: secret/web-credentials created
sections.note: Then in values: auth:\n  existingSecret: web-credentials (chart specific).

sections.title: About this example: OCI registries
sections.body: Helm 3.8+ supports storing charts in OCI registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, Harbor), which removes the need for a separate repository server and uses the same credentials as container images. You use `oci://` URLs directly, without `helm repo add`. Pin the version on every pull or install, because OCI references have no index to search.

sections.title: OCI workflow
sections.code:
helm registry login ghcr.io -u ali --password-stdin < token.txt
helm package ./web --version 1.4.0
helm push web-1.4.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/example/charts
helm show chart oci://ghcr.io/example/charts/web --version 1.4.0 | head -3
helm install web oci://ghcr.io/example/charts/web --version 1.4.0 -n demo
sections.output:
Login Succeeded
Successfully packaged chart and saved it to: /home/ali/web-1.4.0.tgz
Pushed: ghcr.io/example/charts/web:1.4.0
Digest: sha256:3e0f6a1d2b8c91c4a5d7e0b3f4c6a8d9e1b2c3d4f5a6b7c8d9e0f1a2b3c4d5e6
apiVersion: v2
name: web
NAME: web
STATUS: deployed
REVISION: 1

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.body: Installing unpinned charts; putting passwords in values-prod.yaml; using `--reuse-values` instead of a complete values set; letting different engineers deploy from laptops with different local files; treating `helm lint` as enough (it checks chart structure, not whether your cluster accepts the result). Add `helm template | kubectl apply --dry-run=server -f -` and `helm diff` to CI.

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: Pin chart and image versions, keep layered values files in Git, store secrets outside values (existing Secrets, operators, SOPS), review `helm diff` output before every upgrade, deploy with `--atomic`, and prefer OCI registries for your own charts. The final lesson is a troubleshooting playbook for when a release still goes wrong.

questions.question: Why pin the chart version?
options: So deployments are reproducible and upgrades deliberate
questions.explain: Otherwise the newest chart is used, changing what is deployed.

questions.question: Where are values visible after installing?
options: In the release Secret and helm get values
questions.explain: Anyone who can read the release Secret can see them.

questions.question: What does helm diff compare?
options: A proposed upgrade and the live release
questions.explain: It renders the new revision and diffs it against the deployed manifest.

questions.question: How do you reference a chart in an OCI registry?
questions.explain: OCI references are used directly without repo add.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Helm: failed releases and common errors
lessons.summary: A symptom-driven playbook: rendering errors, 'cannot re-use a name', failed and pending-upgrade releases, stuck hooks, timeouts and ownership conflicts.
objectives: Separate rendering errors from cluster errors
Fix 'cannot re-use a name that is still in use'
Recover releases stuck in failed or pending-* states
Diagnose stuck hooks, timeouts and 'exists and cannot be imported'

sections.title: About this example: rendering errors
sections.body: Helm failures fall into three layers: **render** errors (bad values or templates, before anything is sent), **API** errors (the cluster rejects an object) and **rollout** errors (objects accepted, Pods never ready, visible with --wait). `helm template` isolates the first, `--dry-run=server` the second, `kubectl describe` the third. This render error names the template file and line, and the value path involved. Here the values file has `replicaCount` as a string with a typo'd key, and the Service template reads a missing map. Fix by comparing with `helm show values`; run `helm lint` and `helm template --debug` to see the partially rendered output.

sections.title: render errors
sections.code:
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-bad.yaml
helm lint ./web -f values-bad.yaml
helm template web bitnami/nginx -f values-bad.yaml --debug | tail -5
sections.output:
Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: template: nginx/templates/svc.yaml:12:25: executing "nginx/templates/svc.yaml" at <.Values.service.port>: nil pointer evaluating interface {}.port
==> Linting ./web
[ERROR] values.yaml: - (root): Invalid type. Expected: object, given: string
[ERROR] templates/: values don't meet the specifications of the schema(s) in the chart
Error: 1 chart(s) linted, 1 chart(s) failed
sections.note: A nil pointer on .Values.x.y usually means a parent key was replaced (for example service: ClusterIP instead of service.type).

sections.title: About this example: cannot re-use a name and ownership conflicts
sections.body: This error means a release called `web` already exists in the namespace, in any state including `failed` or `uninstalled` with history kept. Look with `helm list -a`. Decide: upgrade it (use `upgrade --install`), remove it, or pick another name. Release names are unique per namespace, so the same name in a different namespace is fine.

sections.title: name and ownership conflicts
sections.code:
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n demo
helm list -a -n demo
helm uninstall web -n demo
kubectl create service clusterip web-nginx --tcp=80:80 -n demo
helm install web bitnami/nginx -n demo
sections.output:
Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: cannot re-use a name that is still in use
NAME  NAMESPACE  REVISION  UPDATED                                  STATUS    CHART         APP VERSION
web   demo       1         2026-11-13 10:15:42.1 +0000 UTC          failed    nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1
release "web" uninstalled
service/web-nginx created
Error: INSTALLATION FAILED: Unable to continue with install: Service "web-nginx" in namespace "demo" exists and cannot be imported into the current release: invalid ownership metadata; label validation error: missing key "app.kubernetes.io/managed-by": must be set to "Helm"; annotation validation error: missing key "meta.helm.sh/release-name": must be set to "web"
sections.note: Name conflict: upgrade, uninstall or rename. Ownership conflict: delete the foreign object, or adopt it by setting label app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=Helm and annotations meta.helm.sh/release-name and meta.helm.sh/release-namespace.

sections.title: About this example: failed and pending-upgrade releases
sections.body: A `failed` release can be fixed by running a corrected `helm upgrade` or rolled back. `pending-upgrade` or `pending-install` that never clears means the Helm client was killed (CI cancelled, laptop closed) mid-operation, and Helm now refuses with 'another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress'. First confirm no process is still running, then roll back to the last good revision, which clears the lock.

sections.title: stuck pending release
sections.code:
helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx -n demo -f values-demo.yaml
helm history web -n demo | tail -3
helm rollback web 4 -n demo --wait
sections.output:
Error: UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress
REVISION  UPDATED                   STATUS           CHART         APP VERSION  DESCRIPTION
4         Thu Nov 13 11:02:14 2026  deployed         nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Upgrade complete
5         Thu Nov 13 11:20:05 2026  pending-upgrade  nginx-18.2.4  1.27.1       Preparing upgrade
Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
sections.note: If no good revision exists, delete the stuck release Secret (kubectl delete secret sh.helm.release.v1.web.v5 -n demo) as a last resort, after backing it up.

sections.title: About this example: stuck hooks and timeouts
sections.body: Hooks are Jobs or Pods that charts run at points like pre-install or post-upgrade (for example a database migration). A hook that never completes blocks the release until `--timeout`. Find the hook Job, read its logs and delete it if it is dead; with `--atomic` the rollback also waits for hooks. For rollout timeouts, inspect Pods rather than Helm.

sections.title: debugging hooks and rollouts
sections.code:
helm get hooks web -n demo | grep -E 'kind|name:|helm.sh/hook'
kubectl get jobs,pods -n demo
kubectl logs job/web-migrate -n demo --tail=3
kubectl describe pod -n demo -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=web | grep -A4 Events
sections.output:
name: web-migrate
  kind: Job
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
NAME                    COMPLETIONS   DURATION   AGE
job.batch/web-migrate   0/1           9m         9m
NAME                    READY   STATUS             RESTARTS   AGE
pod/web-migrate-4kqzp   0/1     CrashLoopBackOff   6          9m
Error: connection to db:5432 refused
Events:
  Warning  BackOff  3m  kubelet  Back-off restarting failed container migrate

sections.title: Error to action map
head: Message contains
Layer
First action
rows: helm show values, helm template --debug, helm lint
helm list -a -n NS; upgrade --install or uninstall
Delete the object or add Helm ownership metadata
Confirm no client running; helm rollback to last deployed
context deadline exceeded / timed out waiting
kubectl describe pod, logs; raise --timeout only if the app is genuinely slow
CRDs missing; install CRDs first or check kube version
kubectl config current-context; VPN; kubeconfig path

sections.title: Recap and what comes next
sections.body: You can classify a Helm failure as render, API or rollout, read the exact error, and apply the matching fix: correct values, resolve name or ownership conflicts, roll back stuck pending-* releases, and investigate hooks and Pods. You have completed the course: you can find charts, install and configure releases, inspect and upgrade them safely, roll back, clean up and run Helm with production discipline. Good next steps are writing your own chart with `helm create`, and the Delivery course on GitOps with Argo CD and Flux, which automate these exact commands.

questions.question: What command shows releases in failed state too?
questions.explain: By default helm list hides some states; -a shows all.

questions.question: What does 'another operation is in progress' usually mean?
options: A previous Helm run was interrupted and left pending-*
questions.explain: The release is locked by a pending revision.

questions.question: How do you inspect hooks of a release?
questions.explain: helm get hooks prints hook manifests.

questions.question: A nil pointer error in a template usually indicates:
options: A missing or wrongly typed value
questions.explain: A parent key is missing or replaced by a scalar.
